name: Butter
description: Butter is not toxic to cats, but it is not a food they should eat. It is almost pure fat, and a cat's digestive system is not built to handle a sudden load of fat. A lick of butter from a plate will not harm most cats, but eating a larger amount can cause vomiting, diarrhea, stomach pain and loss of appetite. The more serious risk is pancreatitis, a painful inflammation of the pancreas that can be triggered by a fatty meal and can be life-threatening. Cats that are overweight, diabetic, or have had pancreatitis before are at higher risk. Butter contains only a small amount of lactose, so lactose intolerance is a minor concern compared with the fat. Salted butter adds sodium, and flavoured or compound butters may contain garlic, onion or herbs, which are the real toxic hazards. A small lick needs no treatment. If your cat has eaten a large amount of butter, watch closely for vomiting, lethargy, loss of appetite or a hunched, painful posture over the next one to two days, and contact your veterinarian if any of these appear.
safetyNotes: Not toxic: a lick of plain butter is not harmful to most cats.
Main hazard: Very high fat content; a larger amount can cause vomiting, diarrhea and stomach pain, and may trigger pancreatitis.
Higher risk: Overweight or diabetic cats and cats with a history of pancreatitis; flavoured butters may contain garlic or onion, which are toxic.
Action: No treatment for a lick; after a large amount, watch for vomiting, lethargy, loss of appetite or a painful belly over 1 to 2 days and call a vet if they appear.

symptoms.name: Vomiting, diarrhea and stomach pain
symptoms.onset: Within a few hours of eating a larger amount
symptoms.notes: Caused by the sudden load of fat. Usually resolves within a day.

symptoms.name: Pancreatitis (persistent vomiting, lethargy, loss of appetite, painful belly)
symptoms.onset: 12 to 48 hours after a fatty meal
symptoms.notes: A fatty meal can trigger inflammation of the pancreas, which can be life-threatening. Overweight or diabetic cats and cats with previous pancreatitis are most at risk. Needs veterinary treatment.
